newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian banks boost gold buying role-state reserve.
newsitem.headline: Russian banks boost gold buying role-state reserve.

text.p: Russian banks are playing an increasingly active role in buying gold but they still pale in comparison to the dominant part played by the Central Bank and the state strategic reserve, a reserve official said Wednesday.

"Over three tonnes of gold have been bought by commercial banks since the beginning of this year alone," said Boris Pozdnyakov, deputy head at the state strategic reserves, known as GosKhran or GosFond.
He said this was well above the volume commercial banks had bought by mid-March in recent years.
Commercial banks are becoming bigger players in Russia's gold industry overall, partly through financing production. Many miners are struggling as state debts to them mount.
The government is borrowing 2.8 trillion roubles from 11 commercial banks at between 1.5 to 6.0 percent interest a year to fund gold and precious stone mining in 1997.
The banks were willing to accept such low interest rates to get into the gold sector in the hope of acquiring more business when Russia's market is liberalised, bankers have said.
One senior industry source at the conference said producers welcomed a more active role by commercial banks in the sector, but warned against handing too much control to them too quickly.
"We favour the gradual liberalisation of the gold market," he said. "It would not be right for commercial banks to become too powerful in the future."
Despite new funds being made available, small, less profitable gold producing operations in Russia would struggle to survive, Pozdnyakov said.
"The analysis of some companies shows that a lot of gold producers cannot survive under current conditions," he said.
"Larger companies producing more than one tonne of gold (annually) will be able to carry on in the future."
Pozdnyakov said that GosFond was aiming to buy 110 tonnes of gold from Russian producers in 1997.

Central Bank deputy chairman Sergei Aleksashenko was quoted earlier on Wednesday by Interfax news agency as that over 1997 and 1998 saying the bank aimed to increase its bullion reserves by 90 tonnes a year.
The Central Bank said it had 400 tonnes of gold at the end of January.

Russia's Central Bank buys gold for its reserves mainly from GosKhran, but also from commercial banks, said Andrei Kulikov, deputy head of precious metals operations at the bank. He said GosKhran had the sole right to buy precious metals directly from producers in Russia.

Russian gold output last year is estimated at 100 to 124 tonnes. Kulikov also said that the Central Bank had boosted gold reserves in 1996 by around 90 tonnes, and a continuation of that rate of replenishment was likely this year.
"It would be normal for us to do the same again this year," he said.
But the industry source voiced scepticism.
"This is the stated plan, but I have my doubts," he said. "After all, the trend in many other countries is to do exactly the opposite."

Some western European central banks released gold onto the market in the last year or so and bullion traders are bracing themselves for more sales as the banks try to raise money to help countries qualify for the European Union single currency.
--Mike Collett-White, Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520
